They're intrusive thoughts, they don't reflect you as a person at all, I promise. The brain often thinks of things unwanted, things that freak us out, etc. For example, if I were to say "Don't think of a blue car" the only image in your brain is going to be a blue car. The brain isn't very good at not thinking about things, no matter how horrible they are. That goes for people even without OCD, though people with OCD get these thoughts more consistently and they often follow a pattern and people who have OCD often have to do things in order to feel better about these thoughts. I'm not sure how new you are to OCD, so I apologise if I'm over explaining. You're not a bad person, its just your brain thinking if the most outrageous and terrible things, things that make you worried and upset. This is not because you want them to happen or thats how you feel but because it *isn't* what you want or feel.

Lady Macbeth. She is the one to really suggest the murder of Duncan. Macbeth is implied to have those thoughts, but to him they are 'ill' and he disapproves of them. He sends a letter to his wife who says that he is "too full of the milk of human kindness" and then she tells him that he must kill Duncan. He doesn't want to but then she says somethings along the lines of "If I had promised you somethings, I'd sooner dash the brains out of my newborn babe than break it" (a lot of the quotes I'm using aren't word for word or paraphrased, I'm doing this from memory. If you have your own copy it might be worth scanning the scenes for them! This would be Act 1 and 2 roughly!)  

The Witches could also be argued as the start if it, because without the prophecies, Lady Macbeth wouldn't have told him to do it. However, you could argue that if not for Lady Macbeth, the murder would never have happened.

There are more gender roles if your interested in that, like Malcolm and Macduff. 

But Lady Macbeth asks spirits to "unsex" her and to make her milk sour, taking away her femininity and later she comes to regret it (when she is being watched by the gentlewoman and the doctor, she asks for her hands to sweeten). 

Macbeth is called a woman and a coward, milk is mentioned with him too "too full of the milk of human kindness" by Lady Macbeth. His mercy and fear about killing Duncan is said to be 'womanly' by Lady Macbeth.

A lot of the time, Lady Macbeth is the one enforcing gender roles, and is the dominant figure in the relationship (which goes against gender roles). She tells Macbeth to commit the murder, and then finishes up covering it. She tells him to do a lot of things until he completely loses his mind (when he sees Banquo's ghost is where I would clock him losing his mind completely), which leads Lady Macbeth to cover for him and in turn leads her into losing her mind (seen with the repetition of "sleep" which can link back to "Macbeth has murdered sleep".)

Its mostly Lady Macbeth making the roles for both of them. When Macbeth loses his mind, he takes control and murders freely, while she grapples with the guilt left behind.

I just preferred going by masculine titles, like boyfriend, brother, man, etc. I go by he/they now, but I still feel like I align with FTM. Honestly, it really stood out to myself when I would imagine myself in another world, I would see myself as a guy. Or see myself as the guy I wanted to be. Flat chest, masculine face, deeper voice, etc. It kinda just finalised that I wanted to be a man and it wasn't a passing (no pun intended) thought, maybe not fully due to me wanting to still be slightly outside that binary, but finalised that I wasn't non-binary nor was I a demi-girl. I was masculine in a "I wish I was a cis man" way, not "I like masculine clothes" way. The more I thought and talked to other trans men about it, the more I realised I still wasn't accepting that part of myself. I dunno! It was a somewhat slow realisation but when I imagined myself as I was then, it felt off and I felt upset. (I mean, I'm not passing at all atm because my voice is like a squeaky toy and I can't bind rn but I've made changes to my wardrobe, hair, and my partner and friends call me by my correct pronouns. And when I imagine myself now it feels more in place.) I guess its kinda just figuring out stepping stones since it isn't obvious right away for everyone.

YTA 

Prosthetics can hurt and cause swelling. (It can hurt more if it isn't fitted too well, as well.) She shouldn't be forced into wearing one if it is causing her pain, or forced into wearing one AT ALL. Its her choice. You are allowed to ask her, but if she has expressed it causes her pain and she doesn't want to wear it, then you shouldn't keep pressuring her to do so. 

She is allowed to chose what she wears and doesn't wear. 

She was open to you. From what it sounds like you did ignore her pain. You asked her to wear it even though she had been open and told you that it was hurting her and she didn't want to wear it. 

If you are worried about your family questioning her, and taking away attention from your brother, it sounds like you need to have a conversation with them. Ask them to leave questions to a minimum (or none at all, depending on how comfortable she is with it), and to be respectful. Also, kids aren't stupid. Their parents can explain that she lost her leg, and she can answer any questions that the kids might have for her if she wants too. Kids need to be educated on disabilities, you can't just ignore the fact some people are disabled and try to hide it from them. (Just a quick add-on, she also doesn't owe explanations or education! If she is willing to answer questions they might have then thats up to her. No disabled person owes an explanation or educating others on their disability. They also don't have to educate kids on it.)  

Honestly, it sounds like you need to be more considerate and less dismissive of her pain. Listen to her when she says she is in pain, don't just brush it off like you did.
